hook: The same people who hid their faces on their own dating profiles judged everyone else’s mostly by the face.
lede: A dating profile is a first impression built in advance: six photos and a few lines of text, arranged for a stranger who will decide with a swipe. We asked 20 experienced dating-app users in China to build one in front of us, on a Tinder account we set up and never published, and to think aloud with every choice. What they described was not a record of who they are, but a careful negotiation between privacy, desire and the person they imagine themselves to be.

stats.label: experienced dating-app users, each building a profile as we watched
photos each participant chose and ordered, for a profile never uploaded
age range of participants, all college-educated
persona strategies, from meeting expectations to crafting intrigue

chapters.title: A face in one of nine squares
paragraphs: Dating photos are usually about appearance and physique. Our participants cared more about atmosphere. They used body language, lighting, negative space and blur to make a stranger want to look closer, and some kept their faces almost out of the picture. P3 never posted clear front-face photos; if she included a flattering one, she put it last, so that only someone interested enough to keep swiping would see her face.

Hiding was also protection. Some feared being recognized by friends or family on the same app, which they found embarrassing. P4 would not post a graduation picture: “I’d rather share it with friends or family, not strangers.” P8 kept her face near the edge of the frame, and had a precise rule for how much of it to show.

quote.text: Really, when I took photos, the phone screen had nine grids, and my face could only occupy one grid. That is all the facial exposure I showed in the picture.

figures.caption: Photos P8 uploaded: (a) no face and plenty of blank space; (b) a swing that conveys body language; (c) her face fills one of the camera’s nine grid cells, a teddy bear the rest.

chapters.title: The first photo is the facade
paragraphs: Photo order was strategy. Apps show one person at a time, and only the first photo at first, so that photo became the profile’s “facade”. Some participants followed a striking first photo with humorous or quirky ones, to soften the distance that good looks can create. Others used photos as filters: P14 chose sports photos to draw people who share the interest, and P9 recommended everyday shots, like a favorite food, because they make it easy to start talking about the best places to eat it.

The most deliberate personas were built from small, odd details. P4 listed astrology as a hobby because it is a little niche and a little mysterious, and people might ask about it. She also wrote “only talk until 10 pm” on her profile, reasoning that most people use dating apps late at night, so someone who sleeps early stands out.

quote.text: We use “only talk until 10 pm” to create a persona that goes to bed early, which is a very niche persona. Don’t you ever wonder why a person goes to bed so early?

chapters.title: A lighter me in my mind
paragraphs: Every profile bent toward someone’s expectations. P1, who had used dating apps in China and in Sweden, left out her body size in China, where she was considered a bit overweight, but listed it in Sweden, where her weight was considered average. Although she described herself as introverted, in Sweden she played up her love of nature and the outdoors, because that seemed to be what people there expected. P4, looking for a serious relationship, chose photos with less skin exposure in China, to avoid signaling that she wanted only a sexual one.

Other exaggerations came from within. P16 posted photos his friends said were edited too much: “People on online dating didn’t know what you looked like anyway.” P12, unhappy with his weight, wrote down a lower number: “Maybe I have always imagined a lighter me in my mind.” He had attended a university ranked 73 in China, but his profile named one of the country’s top 10, a choice he traced to his own “cult of academic qualifications”. That one, he admitted, he feared being caught out on. The weight, he insisted, was still real: an “unfalsifiable proposition and deviation within a reasonable range”.

quote.text: It’s not intentional. It may be subconscious. It’s a habit. I may have lied to myself for too long and have taken it as reality.

chapters.title: Showing the partner you hope to find
paragraphs: The most striking pattern was a mirror. Participants built profiles around the partner they wanted, displaying in themselves the traits they hoped to find. P1 wanted someone smart, so she highlighted her education; she wanted someone with similar hobbies and lifestyle, so she showed her cooking and photography, her drinking and smoking.

We describe this as a cyclical paradigm: “I show what I value; I attract people who like what I show; I discern those I attract whether have traits I value.” Even authenticity was arranged with care. P8 photographed a scene alongside her own sketch of it, because a talent should appear woven into a life rather than demonstrated like a selfie in the gym mirror. P4 preferred landscapes she had shot to posed portraits, because a landscape means “you sincerely think that moment is beautiful, and it touches you.”

quote.text: I like people who are smart, and I also hope that I can show that I am very smart.

figures.caption: Authenticity, arranged: (a) scenery with P8’s own sketch of it; (b) a landscape versus a photo with a person, as P4 described; (c) P3’s photos from different periods and styles, which made people curious.

chapters.title: Reading strangers for signs of truth
paragraphs: Turn the screen around and the same participants became detectives. They distrusted photos that looked “cut out of a magazine”, sets of pictures that were inconsistent with each other, images that were blurry or low-quality, and displays of wealth. P5 had no interest in “a photo taken inside a Lamborghini, wearing Dior and a Rolex watch.” P13 ran suspiciously perfect photos through Baidu image search, and P4 grew wary when a face showed no play of light and shadow.

First impressions still ran on looks: most participants started with appearance and height. Yet small cues could change everything. P1 loved photos with animals. P3 was drawn to a Swedish man working on sea turtle protection whose first photo showed a baby turtle on his face; she felt she had to talk to him. Words were contested. P3 found “photos are more believable than words”, yet also felt that words can reveal whether someone is a misanthrope.

quote.text: If the face looks good, I continue browsing; if not, I stop.

chapters.title: Backstage, but already on stage
paragraphs: Put the two halves together and a double standard appears. Participants hid their own faces yet judged others mainly by appearance. They used blurred or side-view photos for privacy, yet read blur in others’ photos as a sign of falsehood. They demanded authenticity while exaggerating themselves “to an acceptable extent”. Contradictory at first glance, it reflects a balance between self-protection, platform norms and the quest for authenticity in others.

Goffman described social life as a performance, with a front stage for the audience and a backstage for the real self. Our participants suggest a third mode: they believed they were presenting their backstage selves, but were already on the front stage, and they were their own audience. For platforms, this points to three design directions.
points: Two-stage profiles: a curated first layer, with more revealed as chat time accumulates, easing the pressure on anyone wary of being judged at first sight, including people with “invisible” disabilities and transgender users
Searchable matching attributes, such as niche hobbies, without overwhelming users with choice
Visible common ground, such as cities visited, restaurants reviewed or favorite animations, drawn from users’ other social media accounts

takeaways: A dating profile is less a record than a projection: people present the self they imagine, and the partner they hope to attract.
Hiding and revealing are both strategies. Limiting the face can protect privacy and invite curiosity at the same time.
Platforms can support honest self-presentation by letting people reveal themselves in stages and by making real common ground visible.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: Semi-structured interviews (30–60 minutes) with live, think-aloud profile construction

facts.label: Participants
facts.value: 20 college-educated young adults in China (11 female, 9 male), aged 22–33; seven had lived or studied abroad

facts.label: Profile template
facts.value: Tinder’s profile-making interface on a researcher-created account; no profile was uploaded

facts.label: Limitations
facts.value: Chinese college-educated users only; self-reported data; limited attention to text, platform differences and photo editing

facts.label: Follow-up work
facts.value: Informed CARBON COPY, the team’s artwork about a fake dating platform whose AI-written profiles mimic real users’ language
